summary: The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump located in the middle mediastinum. It consists of two atria (receiving chambers) and two ventricles (pumping chambers). The wall comprises three layers: the outer epicardium (visceral pericardium), the thick muscular myocardium, and the inner endocardium.

sections.p: The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump located in the middle mediastinum. It consists of two atria (receiving chambers) and two ventricles (pumping chambers). The wall comprises three layers: the outer epicardium (visceral pericardium), the thick muscular myocardium, and the inner endocardium.

b: Apex: Formed by the left ventricle, located in the 5th left intercostal space, midclavicular line.
Base: Primarily formed by the left atrium, facing posteriorly.
Sternocostal (Anterior) Surface: Mainly formed by the right ventricle.
Diaphragmatic (Inferior) Surface: Formed by both ventricles, primarily the left.
Atrioventricular (AV) Valves: Tricuspid (right) and Mitral (left). Supported by chordae tendineae and papillary muscles to prevent regurgitation during systole.
Semilunar Valves: Pulmonary and Aortic. These prevent backflow from the great vessels during diastole.
Right Coronary Artery (RCA): Supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, SA node (60%), and AV node (80%).
Left Coronary Artery (LCA): Divides into the Left Anterior Descending (LAD), supplying the anterior septum and apex, and the Circumflex artery, supplying the left atrium and posterior left ventricle.

sections.p: Understanding heart anatomy is essential for interpreting Chest X-rays (cardiac silhouette) and diagnosing conditions like heart failure, valvular heart disease, and myocardial infarction.

b: Auricles vs Atria: Auricles are small, muscular pouches projecting from the atria, while atria are the main receiving chambers.
Right vs Left Ventricle walls: The left ventricle is three times thicker than the right to overcome high systemic vascular resistance.
Dextrocardia: In this congenital condition, the heart is mirrored on the right side, which can lead to incorrect electrode placement during ECGs.
Referred pain: Cardiac ischemia often presents as pain in the left arm or jaw due to shared spinal cord segments (T1-T5).

faq.q: What defines the 'base' of the heart?
faq.a: The base is the posterior aspect, formed mainly by the left atrium and a small part of the right atrium, facing the vertebrae.

faq.q: Which coronary artery is usually dominant?
faq.a: The right coronary artery is dominant in approximately 70% of people, meaning it gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery.

faq.q: Where is the apex beat normally palpated?
faq.a: It is typically found in the left fifth intercostal space, along the midclavicular line.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect focused cardiac history and perform a systematic physical exam, noting that many findings are non‑specific and must be interpreted in context.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a tiered approach, prioritising tests that are available and have clear diagnostic thresholds; when unavailable, rely on clinical judgment and alternative modalities.
b: ECG – first line for chest pain and arrhythmia; look for ST changes, Q waves, arrhythmias. A new Q wave in V1‑V4 suggests anterior MI.

t.b: Shows cardiac silhouette size, pulmonary vascular congestion, pleural effusion. A cardiothoracic ratio >0.5 suggests cardiomegaly.

Answers: chamber size, wall thickness, ejection fraction, valve function, pulmonary artery pressure (via TR velocity). EF <40% indicates systolic failure; TR velocity >3.4 m/s suggests pulmonary hypertension.

Direct measurement of mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP). mPAP >20 mmHg at rest defines pulmonary hypertension per ESC/ERS 2022. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure >15 mmHg indicates left heart disease.
Elevated BNP >100 pg/mL (or NT‑proBNP >300 pg/mL) supports heart failure diagnosis; levels >1000 pg/mL correlate with severe HF.
SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension; <1.1 g/dL suggests non‑portal causes of ascites.
Rule out COPD/asthma; FEV1/FVC <70% indicates obstructive disease.
Detects pulmonary embolism; absence of embolus with clinical suspicion may favour heart failure.
CBC, electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, hepatitis serology; abnormal LFTs may mimic cardiac symptoms.
Use bedside ultrasound for cardiac function; use portable ECG; rely on clinical scoring systems (e.g., Framingham, Wells) to estimate probability.

sections.p: Apply current guideline criteria to classify heart disease severity and guide management.
b: Heart failure with reduced EF (HFrEF): EF <40%; 1) NYHA class I‑IV; 2) BNP >100 pg/mL; 3) LVEF <40% on echo.

t.b: WHO Group 1 (PAH): mPAP >20 mmHg, PAWP ≤15 mmHg, PVR >3 WU; Group 2 (left heart disease): PAWP >15 mmHg; Group 3 (lung disease): hypoxia; Group 4 (chronic thromboembolic); Group 5 (miscellaneous).

sections.p: Differentiate cardiac causes from mimics using key distinguishing features.
b: Pulmonary embolism – sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia; CT angiography confirms; ECG may show S1Q3T3 pattern.

t.b: Beck's triad: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, JVD; pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; echo shows pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse.
Severe tearing chest pain radiating to back; CT angiography confirms; ECG may show ST elevation in aVR.
Wheezing, prolonged expiratory phase; ABG shows hypoxia; spirometry shows FEV1/FVC <70%.
Right‑sided S3, hepatomegaly, ascites; liver enzymes mildly raised; imaging shows enlarged liver.

sections.p: Treat heart failure and its complications in a structured ladder, prioritising haemodynamic stability, definitive therapy, monitoring and escalation.
b: 1. Immediate assessment of airway, breathing and circulation; secure airway if respiratory failure.
2. Start intravenous loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) to relieve pulmonary congestion; avoid diuretics only if TACO suspected – they are first‑line.
3. If pulmonary hypertension present, initiate pulmonary vasodilator (e.g., inhaled nitric oxide) and consider endothelin receptor antagonist if chronic.
4. Provide inotropes (dobutamine or milrinone) for low output states; avoid if severe hypotension.
5. Monitor urine output, JVP, oxygen saturation and serial ECGs; adjust diuretics to maintain euvolemia.
6. Escalate to mechanical support (intra‑aortic balloon pump or ECMO) if refractory shock or arrhythmia.
7. Refer to cardiology or transplant centre when surgical valve repair, LVAD or transplant is indicated.

t.b: Assess for obstruction; intubate if SpO2 <90% or altered mental status.
Give oxygen to keep SpO2 >94%; use CPAP if pulmonary edema persists.
Check pulse, BP, JVP; start vasopressor if systolic <90 mmHg.
Use IV loop diuretics to remove excess fluid; avoid if TACO suspected but treat with diuretics first.
Dobutamine improves CO; avoid in severe hypotension.
IABP lowers LV afterload; ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Recognise key adverse effects, interactions and management steps for common heart failure drugs.
b: Loop diuretics cause electrolyte loss; replace potassium and magnesium and monitor serum levels.
ACE inhibitors/ARBs can precipitate hyperkalaemia; check potassium and creatinine before each dose.
Beta‑blockers may worsen bradycardia; titrate slowly and avoid in severe hypotension.
Digoxin toxicity presents with nausea, visual changes; monitor serum levels and renal function.
Statins may cause myopathy; advise patients to report muscle pain and check CK if symptomatic.
NSAIDs raise BP and worsen renal function; avoid in advanced heart failure.

t.b: Check K+, Mg2+, Ca2+ every 2–3 days when starting or increasing diuretics.
Check serum creatinine and eGFR before ACEI/ARB initiation; hold if >30% rise.
Maintain serum level 0.5–1.0 ng/mL; adjust for renal impairment.
Avoid NSAIDs with ACEI/ARB; avoid CYP3A4 inhibitors with statins.
Nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances = digoxin; muscle pain = statin; hypotension = beta‑blocker.

sections.p: Identify red flags that require urgent escalation or specialist referral.
b: Cardiogenic shock – persistent hypotension despite fluids and inotropes.
Pulmonary edema unresponsive to diuretics – consider mechanical ventilation or IABP.
Severe arrhythmias (VT/VF) – immediate defibrillation and antiarrhythmic therapy.
Acute kidney injury – stop nephrotoxic drugs and consider dialysis.
Worsening liver function – evaluate for congestive hepatopathy and adjust diuretics.

t.b: Systolic BP <90 mmHg, cold extremities, oliguria; refer to ICU.
Unresponsive to diuretics; intubate and consider IABP.
VT/VF – defibrillate; SVT – adenosine or beta‑blocker.
Rise in creatinine >50% from baseline; hold ACEI/ARB.
Elevated transaminases >5× ULN; assess for congestion.

sections.p: Adjust assessment and management in the presence of comorbidities common in low‑resource settings.
b: HIV – opportunistic infections can mimic heart failure; use CD4 count to guide therapy.
TB – miliary disease may cause pericardial effusion; treat with anti‑TB drugs and consider pericardiocentesis.
Malnutrition – low albumin reduces drug binding; monitor drug levels.
Diabetes – glycaemic control affects fluid balance; avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
Herbal remedies – some contain quinine or diuretics; review for interactions.
Alcohol – chronic use worsens cardiomyopathy; counsel cessation.
Renal failure – dose adjust diuretics and ACEI/ARB; avoid NSAIDs.
Liver failure – reduce statins and ACEI/ARB; monitor transaminases.
Elderly – frailty increases sensitivity to diuretics; monitor electrolytes closely.

sections.p: Tailor management for children, pregnancy, elderly, HIV patients and low‑resource settings.
b: Children – use age‑appropriate dosing; monitor growth and developmental milestones.
Pregnancy – avoid ACEI/ARB in 2nd/3rd trimester; use labetalol or methyldopa for hypertension.
Elderly – start low dose, titrate slowly; watch for orthostatic hypotension.
HIV – consider drug–drug interactions with antiretrovirals; monitor CD4 and viral load.
Low‑resource – prioritize affordable diuretics, use clinical signs when labs unavailable; use point‑of‑care ultrasound for pericardial effusion.

facts: Mean pulmonary arterial pressure >20 mmHg at rest defines pulmonary hypertension (ESC/ERS 2022).
Right atrial pressure >10 mmHg suggests right‑sided failure.
Transudative pleural effusion: pleural fluid protein/serum protein ≤0.5 and LDH ratio ≤0.6.
Cardiac output normal range 4.0–8.0 L/min; low output <4.0 L/min indicates pump failure.
Left ventricular wall thickness >12 mm on echo is abnormal hypertrophy.
Tricuspid regurgitation jet velocity >2.8 m/s suggests severe regurgitation.
Serum‑ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension.
TACO (transfusion‑associated circulatory overload) is treated first‑line with IV loop diuretics.
Pulmonary regurgitation produces an early diastolic decrescendo murmur, not holosystolic.
Down syndrome: ~40–50% have congenital heart disease, most commonly AV septal defect.

vivas.q: Define the diagnostic threshold for pulmonary hypertension according to the 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines.
vivas.a: Mean pulmonary arterial pressure >20 mmHg at rest measured by right‑heart catheterisation.

vivas.q: What bedside test distinguishes transudate from exudate when laboratory analysis is unavailable?
vivas.a: Pleural fluid appearance and gross protein content; a clear, watery fluid with low protein suggests transudate.

vivas.q: Explain why intravenous loop diuretics are the first‑line treatment for TACO.
vivas.a: They rapidly mobilise excess intravascular volume, reducing pulmonary capillary pressure and relieving pulmonary oedema.

vivas.q: How do you elicit a right‑sided S3 and what does it indicate?
vivas.a: Place the bell at the lower left sternal border during rapid filling; a low‑frequency sound indicates volume overload of the right ventricle.

vivas.q: Why is pulmonary regurgitation an early diastolic murmur and not holosystolic?
vivas.a: Regurgitation occurs when the pulmonary valve fails to close during diastole, producing a decrescendo sound after S2.

vivas.q: Interpret a pleural fluid analysis: protein 2.1 g/dL, serum protein 7.0 g/dL, LDH fluid 88 U/L, serum LDH 300 U/L.
vivas.a: Fluid/serum protein ratio 0.30 and LDH ratio 0.29 – both below transudate cut‑offs; this is a transudative effusion, most likely due to heart failure.

vivas.q: A transplant patient’s sputum shows oval budding yeasts with pseudohyphae. What is the significance?
vivas.a: Findings are characteristic of Candida species; in a transplant recipient they indicate opportunistic infection requiring antifungal therapy.

vivas.q: What is the most likely type of pleural effusion in a right‑sided heart failure patient?
vivas.a: Transudative effusion due to increased hydrostatic pressure in the systemic circulation.

vivas.q: A 16‑year‑old with a left chest stab wound is hypotensive, lungs clear, heart sounds faint. What is the most useful immediate treatment?
vivas.a: Emergency pericardiocentesis to relieve cardiac tamponade.

vivas.q: During the second unit of packed red cells a patient develops dyspnoea, hypertension and raised JVP with pulmonary oedema on CXR. What complication is this?
What percentage of individuals with Down syndrome have congenital heart disease?
vivas.a: Approximately 40–50 % of patients, most commonly atrioventricular septal defect.

vivas.q: A 72‑year‑old with LVH, small scarred kidneys and concentric arteriolar thickening dies of basal ganglia bleed. What underlying condition is most likely?
vivas.a: Chronic hypertension leading to hypertensive heart disease and renal arteriolosclerosis.

vivas.q: After 10 years a porcine bioprosthetic valve fails. What pathologic change is expected?
vivas.a: Structural valve degeneration with calcification and leaflet thickening.

vivas.q: Which hepatic acinar zone is most vulnerable to congestion from severe right‑heart failure and why?
vivas.a: Zone 3 (centrilobular) because it receives the least oxygenated blood and is closest to the central vein where congestion occurs.

vivas.q: In right‑heart failure, why is zone 1 relatively spared compared with zone 3?
vivas.a: Zone 1 receives blood directly from the hepatic artery and portal vein with higher oxygen tension, so it is less affected by venous congestion.

vivas.q: List three key history questions for a patient with suspected right‑sided heart failure.
vivas.a: 1) Peripheral oedema onset and progression; 2) Abdominal fullness or ascites; 3) History of left‑sided failure or pulmonary hypertension.

vivas.q: Describe how to perform and interpret the hepatojugular reflux test.
vivas.a: Apply firm pressure over the liver for 10 seconds; a rise >3 cm in JVP that persists indicates impaired right‑ventricular filling.

vivas.q: What is the role of bedside ultrasound in acute right‑heart failure?
vivas.a: Rapid assessment of IVC size and collapsibility, right‑ventricular dilation, and pleural effusions to guide fluid management.

mcqs.q: A 55‑year‑old man with chronic heart failure presents with a right‑sided pleural effusion. Which of the following fluid analyses confirms a transudate?
o: Pleural fluid protein 4.0 g/dL, serum protein 6.0 g/dL
Pleural fluid LDH 250 U/L, serum LDH 300 U/L
Pleural fluid/serum protein ratio 0.3 and LDH ratio 0.29
mcqs.e: Both ratios are below transudate cut‑offs (≤0.5 protein, ≤0.6 LDH).

mcqs.q: Which murmur is characteristic of pulmonary regurgitation?
o: Holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border
Early diastolic decrescendo murmur best heard at left upper sternal border
mcqs.e: Pulmonary regurgitation produces an early diastolic decrescendo sound.

mcqs.q: A patient develops dyspnoea, hypertension and raised JVP during a second unit of blood. Which immediate therapy is most appropriate?
mcqs.e: TACO is managed with rapid IV loop diuretics.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the correct definition of pulmonary hypertension per 2022 guidelines?
mcqs.e: 2022 ESC/ERS lowered the threshold to >20 mmHg.

mcqs.q: A 16‑year‑old with a left chest stab wound is hypotensive, lungs clear, heart sounds faint. Which bedside maneuver is most likely to improve his condition immediately?
mcqs.e: Faint heart sounds with clear lungs suggest tamponade; pericardiocentesis relieves it.

mcqs.q: In right‑heart failure, which hepatic zone shows the highest risk of necrosis due to hypoxia?
mcqs.e: Zone 3 is furthest from oxygen‑rich blood and most affected by congestion.

mcqs.q: Which of the following statements about bioprosthetic valve degeneration is correct after 10 years?
o: Calcification is the primary cause of failure
Structural degeneration is rare before 20 years
Degeneration is unrelated to patient age
mcqs.e: Calcific and fibrotic changes are the main mechanisms of bioprosthetic failure.

mcqs.q: What proportion of Down‑syndrome individuals have congenital heart disease?
mcqs.e: Approximately 40–50 % have CHD, most often AV septal defect.

cases.v: A 58‑year‑old man presents with progressive dyspnoea, peripheral oedema and a loud P2. Echo shows right‑ventricular dilation, tricuspid regurgitation jet velocity 3.2 m/s, and estimated systolic PAP 55 mmHg.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Pulmonary hypertension secondary to left‑sided heart disease.

qs.q: Which bedside test would confirm elevated right‑sided pressures?
qs.a: Hepatojugular reflux – a sustained rise in JVP with abdominal pressure.

cases.v: A 22‑year‑old woman with no prior cardiac history presents with sudden syncope during exertion. Examination reveals a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border radiating to the back. CT angiography shows a large pulmonary embolus.

qs.q: How does the murmur relate to her presentation?
qs.a: Acute right‑ventricular pressure overload produces a functional tricuspid regurgitation murmur.

qs.q: What immediate investigation confirms right‑heart strain?
qs.a: Elevated troponin and BNP together with right‑ventricular dilation on bedside echocardiography.

qs.q: What acute management should be initiated?
qs.a: Systemic thrombolysis (if no contraindication) or catheter‑directed thrombectomy, plus oxygen and fluids cautiously.

mistakes: Confusing the transudate/exudate protein and LDH ratios; always apply ≤0.5 and ≤0.6 cut‑offs respectively.
Assuming diuretics are contraindicated in TACO – they are the primary treatment.
Labeling pulmonary regurgitation as holosystolic; it is an early diastolic murmur.
Using the outdated ≥25 mmHg threshold for pulmonary hypertension.
Neglecting to assess hepatojugular reflux when right‑sided failure is suspected.
Relying solely on pleural fluid appearance without calculating ratios.
Over‑interpreting a mild tricuspid regurgitation jet as severe without quantitative assessment.
Failing to consider HIV or malnutrition as modifiers of cardiac presentation in low‑resource settings.
